name: Anti-Federalists
summary: The Anti-Federalists opposed ratifying the 1787 US Constitution as drafted, fearing it would consolidate the states into one distant national government. They held that free republics must be small, that representatives should be numerous, close to and dependent on ordinary citizens, and that rulers, standing armies and federal taxing power threaten liberty unless limited by explicit rights. Their pressure helped produce the Bill of Rights.
scope: The 1787-88 opponents of the Constitution as represented by the Brutus and Federal Farmer essays, George Mason and Patrick Henry, as summarized by Storing-based scholarship. It covers only the ratification-era political-structure debate; economic, social and modern questions were mostly not addressed and are low-confidence inferences or 0.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Healthcare provision was not a question in 1787-88; a national program would run against their preference for local, limited federal power, so a mild inference of disagreement.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: No wage law existed in the debate; any national wage regulation would be a federal power they distrusted, though some local action fits their small-republic view.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The debate was about government structure, not market theory; adherents were mostly small farmers wary of both merchant interests and government, so they split.

public-ownership.rationale: Not discussed; national ownership of industry would mean the consolidated central power they opposed, and adherents were property-owning farmers.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Opponents feared federal taxing power over citizens generally, while also distrusting merchant and aristocratic elites, so no clear stance on higher taxes on the rich.

unions-good.rationale: Unions did not exist as modern institutions; the tradition's artisans and farmers give no basis for a stance.

property-fundamental.rationale: Federal Farmer wanted rights such as protection from unreasonable search and taxes written down to restrain federal power, implying strong protection of holdings; property as such is inferred.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Corporations were rare and not addressed; suspicion of merchant elites pushes one way and suspicion of federal power the other.

cut-welfare.rationale: No welfare state existed; no source ties the Anti-Federalists to a stance, and local relief versus federal cost cannot be resolved.

worker-ownership.rationale: Not addressed; the movement's base of independent small farmers favors owner-operators, but nothing in sources speaks to collective ownership.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Federal Farmer demanded explicit protection against unreasonable searches and general warrants, reflecting a core distrust of federal power over individual liberty.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Not addressed; adherents were localists who would leave the matter to states, which gives no position on legality as such.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Federal Farmer insists on explicit protection of a free press against federal restraint, so a speech restriction would be viewed with suspicion; inferred for the modern issue.

strong-leader.rationale: Opponents feared the presidency would grow into monarchy and Brutus warned that rulers in a large republic escape popular control; a leader bypassing checks is the opposite of their view.

state-harmful.rationale: They wanted limited republican government, not no government; they relied on state and local government for liberty and order.

limit-guns.rationale: Inferred from their hostility to standing armies; none of the cited sources discusses private gun ownership.

empower-police-military.rationale: Brutus said standing armies have always proved the destruction of liberty; they opposed giving the federal government a standing force.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Not addressed; localism implies leaving it to states but gives no moral stance.

decide-locally.rationale: The federalism encyclopedia says they envisioned a collection of small republics with political power and decision-making kept at the local and state levels.

rehabilitation.rationale: Their criminal-justice concern was procedural rights (jury, counsel, confrontation), not the aim of punishment.

traditional-family.rationale: Not a debate topic; adherents were mostly rural and conventional for the era, a weak inference.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Anachronistic; period adherents held conventional views, but localism would leave it to states, so mild disagreement as inference.

abortion-legal.rationale: Anachronistic and not addressed by the movement; adherents' modern heirs are split.

more-religion-public.rationale: The ratification debate included both religious objections to the lack of a religious test and demands for conscience protection; adherents were divided.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Not a movement concern, and some leading Anti-Federalists were slaveholders; federal action to correct injustice conflicts with their anti-centralism.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Their concern was local self-government and virtue of small communities rather than national culture, which they associated more with states.

gradual-change.rationale: They resisted a rapid, sweeping new constitution yet had just made a revolution; they were reformers defending existing institutions of the Confederation and states, so split.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Not addressed in the ratification debate.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: If a national government was too distant, an international body would be far more so; the tradition prizes local self-rule.

free-trade.rationale: Trade policy was debated as commerce regulation and navigation acts, with adherents divided by region and interest.

nation-first.rationale: Not a central concern; they feared foreign entanglement but their focus was domestic liberty.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Inferred from their fear that military power abroad enlarges the standing force and executive, which destroys liberty.

open-borders.rationale: Not addressed; their emphasis on small, attached communities of shared circumstances points mildly against, as inference.

limit-growth.rationale: Anachronistic; no basis for a position.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Anachronistic; large-scale federal action runs against their preference for local power.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Anachronistic; no basis for a position.

revolution-justified.rationale: They were veterans of the American Revolution and Patrick Henry's tradition of resistance to distant authority; they otherwise sought change through amendments and conventions.

experts-over-public.rationale: Storing's account stresses fear of rule by distant elites and a preference for representatives of the middling sort and citizens participating in governing.

central-planning.rationale: Centralized direction of an economy embodies the consolidated, distant power they rejected.

land-value-tax.rationale: Not addressed; they opposed direct federal taxation, which cuts against but is not about land taxes by states.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; no stance.

basic-income.rationale: Anachronistic; national transfer scheme would require the central taxing power they opposed.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Commerce regulation split adherents by region and trade interest; no unified stance.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Inferred from their distrust of centralised power and of favoured merchant interests.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The movement drew heavily on small farmers and sought to protect rural and agrarian interests against concentrated urban merchant interests.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Not addressed; independent farmers and artisans would not favor abolishing money, as inference.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: No central bank existed to oppose in 1787; Anti-Federalist heirs later opposed one, but the ratification debate is silent.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Representation by middling citizens and neighbors, not state-recognized corporate bodies, was their model; mild inference.

one-party-rule.rationale: They demanded that the people give assent to laws through representatives who truly speak for them; rule by one party is the opposite.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: They feared the presidency would evolve into a monarchy and were republicans who had just thrown off a king.

democracy-best.rationale: Brutus holds that sovereignty must rest with the whole people, though the Anti-Federalists favored a republic with representatives rather than pure democracy.

direct-votes.rationale: They wanted more numerous, closer representatives rather than direct law-making; Brutus accepts assent either directly or through representatives.

workers-councils.rationale: Not addressed; they favored existing states and representative assemblies.

right-to-secede.rationale: They saw the Union as a league of states and feared consolidation, but ratification-era writers did not endorse unilateral secession; split.

natural-rulers.rationale: They feared government by aristocratic elites and wanted representatives from the middling sort.

political-violence-never.rationale: Revolutionary-era veterans who defended armed resistance to tyranny; they did not hold a pacifist stance.

war-builds-character.rationale: Brutus saw standing armies and military power as destructive of liberty; no sourced praise of war.

separate-church-state.rationale: Adherents were split between those wanting a religious test or establishment in states and those insisting on conscience rights.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Adherents ranged from devout Protestants to Enlightenment deists; no common position.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Defense was a public duty they wanted entrusted to militias and state authority, and they saw courts and juries as protection against rulers; privatization lacks any support.

military-superiority.rationale: Brutus argued standing armies destroy liberty; they sought limited federal military power.

class-struggle-history.rationale: They did voice fears of elites against the people, but did not theorize class conflict as history's engine.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Not addressed; they wanted representation of ordinary citizens but not material equalization, an inference.

civilizational-union.rationale: Opposed the union of distant peoples under one government in the American case; mild inference for supranational unions.

self-interest-moral.rationale: They stressed civic virtue but did not condemn private interest; split.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Federal Farmer and Mason pressed for a bill of rights to protect individual liberties from government; the movement was rights-first, though it valued civic virtue.

limit-population.rationale: Not addressed; a frontier-agrarian people was unlikely to favor limits, as inference.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Anachronistic and unaddressed, though agrarian preferences exist.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Inferred from their preference for stable small communities and distrust of disruption.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Inferred from their insistence that representatives be close, accountable and truly speak for the people.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Inferred from their insistence on protection of papers and persons against federal searches.

restore-past-order.rationale: They defended the Articles of Confederation and state powers yet claimed the revolution's republican principles, so mixed.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Brutus argues from principle and from historical lessons about liberty, not outcome pragmatism; weak inference.

direct-action.rationale: They pursued conventions, pamphlets and amendments through the ratifying process.

means-match-ends.rationale: No ratification-era source frames methods versus ends; they used pamphlets and conventions but stated no principle.

return-to-foraging.rationale: No basis, and the movement was agrarian and settled.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from their settled economic life.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Not addressed; property-owning farmers were unlikely to endorse it.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Not addressed; they were property owners, not Marxists.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Concentrated power over any class conflicts with their demand for popular consent and fear of unchecked rulers.

collective-farming.rationale: The movement was based on independent small farmers, and compulsory collective farming opposes their liberty-based politics.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Capitalism as a system and imperialism as its product were not concepts in the 1787 debate.

taxation-theft.rationale: They opposed the federal taxing power and direct federal taxes but accepted taxation by legitimate state governments; they did not call it theft.

harm-principle.rationale: Not addressed; adherents accepted community moral regulation at state level.

individual-rights-only.rationale: They demanded rights guaranteed to individuals, yet also valued collective rights such as jury and militia and state rights; split.

conscription.rationale: Their militia ideal rested on citizens' service in state forces, but they opposed federal power to raise armies; a federal draft would be opposed.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Brutus puts voice and assent of the people first; exit as a check is not part of their case.

state-as-business.rationale: Inferred from their civic republican emphasis on citizens governing, not customers.

positive-liberty.rationale: Not addressed; liberty was understood as protection from government.

organic-representation.rationale: They favored geographic representation by neighbors of the middling sort, rather than corporate bodies, but not parties either.

total-state.rationale: Implied by their fear that a consolidated government would rise above the control of the people; they never discuss a state directing all of life.

national-rebirth.rationale: Not their frame; they defended existing states and the Articles.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Brutus argues a republic cannot survive over a vast territory, so expansion of the union's extent worsens the problem.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: They rejected monarchical or aristocratic authority and based legitimacy on popular assent.

bound-labor.rationale: Some adherents were slaveholders but the tradition stressed freeholding farmers; serfdom unaddressed.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The ratification debate had no epistemological dimension; this modern claim is unaddressed.

universal-morality.rationale: Enlightenment natural rights thinking underlay their bill of rights demands; loosely inferred.

single-common-good.rationale: They held virtue and common good in small republics but also feared that large republics ignore diverse interests; split.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: A Zionist question with no connection to the American ratification debate.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Diaspora return rights were never raised by the 1787-88 opponents of the Constitution.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language revival was not at issue; English was the shared language of both camps.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Not addressed; some inference of participatory attitude.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Not addressed as policy; the debate over federal debt power had mixed interests.

rule-by-example.rationale: They valued civic virtue as a restraint but also demanded written rights and legal limits.

national-self-determination.rationale: Not addressed; they stressed state and local self-government.

force-without-un.rationale: Inferred from fear of military power and executive war-making.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Adherents included religious and rationalist figures.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: No welfare benefits existed for immigrants or citizens to be allocated in 1787.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Public relief was a local matter and work conditions were not discussed in the sources.

class-collaboration.rationale: The sources show fear of elite domination but no theory of employer-worker relations.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Not addressed; their conservative localism contradicts the idea, inferred.

dominated-front.rationale: Nothing in the sources concerns a common front against leading powers.

workers-nation.rationale: Working-class organization was not a ratification-era question.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Not addressed in sources; adherents shared the conventions of the era, though Mercy Otis Warren was a prominent woman writer.

ban-interest.rationale: Usury law was not discussed in the sources used; no position found.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Not addressed; anachronistic; they sought limited federal power.

state-class-instrument.rationale: They feared the state would be captured by elites, but did not hold that this is its essential nature.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Immigrant assimilation was not raised in the sources about the ratification debate.

proportional-representation.rationale: They wanted larger, more numerous representation but the debate concerned geographic representation, not party lists.

national-mission.rationale: Inferred from their view that free republics must be small and local and can't be spread.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: A modern analytical claim; the ratification-era sources do not address it.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The Bill of Rights Institute essay voices their complaint that politicians are out of touch, and the federalism encyclopedia says they saw distant government as easily corrupted because people could not monitor those in power.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Anachronistic; opposed by their liberty-based politics, inferred.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Federal Farmer wanted protections against quartering soldiers and arbitrary searches; accountability inferred.

night-watchman-state.rationale: They wanted a federal government of limited powers but defended broad powers for state governments, so support for minimal government in general is only inferred.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Race-mixing policy was not discussed in the ratification debate sources.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Natural rights language was common, but many held slaves and the sources do not address it.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Socialism is outside the 1787 debate entirely.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: The sources do not frame the United States as a settler colonial project.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Inferred from their preference for state diversity of laws over uniform national rules.

restrict-conversion.rationale: They sought conscience protection against federal power, inferred.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: A religious-politics issue unconnected to the Constitution debate.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: State schools were not a topic in the sources; education was local.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Fear of standing armies and growing central power shows they would reject a state justifying growth by external threat.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Brutus states that the people must give their assent to the laws, directly or through representatives who truly speak for them.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist trade balance goals were not addressed in the Anti-Federalist sources.

population-transfer.rationale: Their demand for rights and procedural protections against government overreach is incompatible with it.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Not addressed; they accepted legitimate state coercion.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Social-Darwinist themes post-date the movement; nothing in the sources addresses it.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Inferred from their emphasis on press and speech protection against government.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: They feared rulers able to oppress citizens and escape popular control, matching a republican concern with arbitrary power.

separated-powers.rationale: Implied by Brutus's insistence that rulers stay responsible to the people and his fear that a few officials would hold command, appointment and revenue powers together.

vanguard-party.rationale: Implied and anachronistic: Brutus grounds legitimacy in the people's assent to laws, not in a disciplined leading party.

priority-to-poor.rationale: They represented small farmers and the middling sort, but sought no poverty program.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: A British housing policy with no connection to the American debate.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Strike law was anachronistic to the ratification debate.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Malthusian causes of poverty were not raised in the sources.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Storing's account says Anti-Federalists thought large, diverse territories could be held only by coercion, so shared circumstances matter to cohesion.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Federal Farmer favored elections, rotation and recall, not lotteries; but he wanted ordinary citizens to hold office.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Federal Farmer insisted on habeas corpus and other guarantees against federal power; suspension would be opposed.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Price fixing was not discussed in the sources, though states had used it during the war.

party-controls-media.rationale: Federal Farmer insisted on a free press against federal restraint.

party-commands-army.rationale: Brutus opposed standing armies and concentrated military control.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; the debate dealt with naturalization as a federal power.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: They wanted representatives from the middling sort, but not specifically at worker pay.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Federal Farmer wanted legislators feeling dependent on voters, not bound to party; inferred.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Anachronistic but implied: they saw even the national union as distant, unresponsive government, so pooling sovereignty further would offend their localism.

head-commands-forces.rationale: They feared the president as monarch-like and opposed unchecked executive command of armies.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Church governance was not part of the constitutional debate sources.

clerical-rule.rationale: Republican popular sovereignty, not clerical rule.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Not addressed; the tradition prized loyalty to the states and people.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Federal Farmer demanded explicit protection of the press; censorship is inferred to be opposed.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Federal Farmer No. 11 demands rotation for federal legislators only; extending it to the president is implied by their fear that the presidency might evolve into a monarchy.

recall-officials.rationale: Federal Farmer explicitly wanted a right to recall members and rotation written into the Constitution.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Inferred from their fear of standing armies and entanglement; period debates did not directly address alliances.

people-in-arms.rationale: Their opposition to standing armies went with preference for citizen militia; the quoted Brutus passage condemns standing armies as destroying liberty.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: The movement drew heavily from farmers and sought to protect rural interests against urban merchants, though virtue was framed politically.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: National reunification across borders did not arise in the debate.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Storing's account describes fear of educated or wealthy elites out of touch with ordinary people.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Cultural relativism was not raised in the sources.

death-penalty.rationale: Not addressed; most of the era accepted it.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Modern curriculum question with no counterpart in the sources.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: A twentieth-century issue not raised in the ratification debate.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Not addressed in the sources about the ratification debate.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Citizenship rules were debated as a federal power but the sources give no stance on descent.

minority-language-support.rationale: Language policy was not addressed in the sources.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Mill-style individuality was not part of the ratification debate.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: International debt relief is outside the sources; domestic debt was debated differently.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Their concern was constitutional structure after independence, not economic transformation.

constituent-assembly.rationale: They called for a second constitutional convention to amend the proposed Constitution before ratification.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Their politics centered on guaranteeing freedoms against government.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Foreign aid was not discussed in the sources.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: They feared a powerful presidency of any kind; the debate on electors and election was mixed.

central-bank-independence.rationale: No central bank existed in 1787 and the sources do not address one.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Not addressed in the sources about the ratification debate.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The sources protect property and rights but do not state a common-good condition.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: The Soviet Union was far outside the movement's horizon.

precautionary-principle.rationale: An environmental doctrine anachronistic to the sources.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Annexation law is not covered by the sources.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Not addressed; opposed to concentrated federal power in either direction.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The sources fear a powerful presidency but do not discuss a ceremonial symbol of unity.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: They saw the union as a league of states and feared federal coercion of states; weak inference.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Their model was union that retains state autonomy over internal matters.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Implied: they feared the presidency might evolve into a monarchy, so a sacred ruler of divine descent is far from their republicanism.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Income tax did not exist; the sources address direct federal taxes only in general.

character-from-environment.rationale: They believed small republics shape civic virtue in citizens, an environmental view of character, loosely inferred.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: They demanded rulers be restrained by the Constitution and bill of rights.

space-expansion.rationale: Anachronistic; nothing in the sources bears on it.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Debate on the Senate: they feared aristocracy in the Senate, but the Federalists used mixed constitutional arguments too, and the Anti-Federalists accepted checks.

leader-cult.rationale: Implied: Brutus wants rulers responsible to the people and removable when they misbehave, which sits badly with venerating a leader as the nation.

equal-parenting.rationale: Family court policy is not covered by the sources.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Socialist-state theory has no link to the movement.

land-redistribution.rationale: The movement was property-owning and small-farmer based, not redistributionist, as inference.

refugee-return.rationale: Refugee return was not addressed in the sources.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Inferred from opposition to enlarged territorial union.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Inferred from their demand for written rights guarantees that produced the Bill of Rights; the cited sources do not discuss religion.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Brutus opposes consolidating distant peoples under one government.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Minority cultural institutions were not addressed in the sources.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Not addressed; the sources concern rights within the American republic generally.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Historical materialism is not part of the sources; the movement argued from political principle.

ban-cartels.rationale: Antitrust was not a ratification-era issue in the sources.

no-bailouts.rationale: Bailouts were not discussed in the sources.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Brutus feared an unaccountable judiciary but also wanted rights protected against rulers; split.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Women's representation was not discussed in the ratification-era sources.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Autarkic blocs were not debated in the sources.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Not addressed; treaty standards are anachronistic.

moral-incentives.rationale: Incentive systems were not discussed in the sources.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Guerrilla-vanguard theory is not in the sources; they relied on conventions and ratification.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: They feared aristocracy and wanted representatives from the middling sort.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Curriculum content was not addressed in the sources.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from consent doctrine.

patriotic-education.rationale: Civic education was valued in republican thought generally, but the sources used do not state a stance on loyalty teaching.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Modern affirmative-action law is not addressed in the sources.

public-money-creation.rationale: Money creation was not debated in the sources used.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Capitalist crisis theory is outside the sources.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Federal Farmer and the broader movement demanded explicit written guarantees such as jury trial and a free press, leading to the Bill of Rights.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Not an issue in 1787-88; the movement had no position on influence over a predecessor empire.

delink-world-market.rationale: Not addressed in the ratification debate; no basis for either answer.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Class exploitation between nations was not discussed in 1787-88; neutral inference.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Not addressed; their stress on local control and individual liberty points both ways.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Colonial-era treaties were not discussed in the ratification debate.

elective-rulers.rationale: They were republicans who feared the new presidency might evolve into a monarchy, and Federal Farmer wanted elected members kept accountable through recall and rotation.

minority-veto.rationale: Unanimity governed under the Articles, but the movement's writers did not argue for individual vetoes; adherents split.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Brutus warns of tyranny from a distant government and the republican tradition permits resistance, but the point is inferred.

parliament-supreme.rationale: They preferred strong, numerous legislatures and feared the executive, which is inferred as support for legislative primacy over a monarch.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Not discussed in the debate, so adherents are inferred as neutral.

animal-use-humane.rationale: The movement was mostly farmers who kept livestock; the humane limit is inferred.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: They distrusted a ruling few, but a duty of the privileged was not argued, so adherents are inferred as split.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Federal Farmer insists that citizens must participate in government to keep liberty, so withdrawal is rejected.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: The claim is anachronistic and the debate never touched on mass culture.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: They feared rulers who govern by force and by influence of the wealthy, but did not theorise consent; inferred as neutral.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: The debate did not address world economic structure.

native-born-offices.rationale: Not a stated issue in the sources; adherents are inferred as neutral.

party-own-road.rationale: Communist parties did not exist; no inference is available.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: They valued a farmer republic's independence and opposed foreign entanglements, so the lean is mild and inferred.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: The movement's equal-citizen republic does not fit ancestry-based rule, but the issue is anachronistic, so this is inferred.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Anachronistic for 1787-88, so no position can be inferred.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Anachronistic for 1787-88, so no position can be inferred.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Anti-Federalists were divided on slavery, with Southern and Northern members on both sides, and the Civil War is anachronistic.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Anachronistic; nothing in the debate bears on it.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Brutus, following Montesquieu, holds that republican institutions suit a small, homogeneous people, so forms differ by society.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Brutus says standing armies have always proved the destruction of liberty and are abhorrent to the spirit of a free republic, so a political role for the army is rejected.

filial-duty.rationale: Not debated in 1787-88; the republican-virtue and household-centred moral outlook of the movement suggests support for family obligations.

office-by-exam.rationale: They wanted officials elected, rotated and answerable to the people, so selection by examination is an inference against their preference.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Not addressed; their fear of distant, consolidated and corruptible power suggests wariness of foreign influence over national assets.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Not addressed; 18th-century divorce required proof of fault or a legislative act, and the movement was morally conservative, so a mild inference of disagreement.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Federal Farmer No. 11 says constituents should retain the power of recalling their agents and judging their conduct, but it does not call for binding instructions.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Not addressed; the independent yeoman self-reliance they prized and distrust of central funds suggest private provision, inferred.

land-use-tenure.rationale: The movement spoke for freehold farmers and the middling sort who owned their land outright; communal or use-based tenure is inferred to be foreign to it.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Their objection to federal taxing power, and demands for popular-house control of money, mean spending should depend on the elected legislature.

single-official-language.rationale: Not addressed; their preference for local self-government and diverse states suggests no enforced single language, inferred.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Not addressed; a localist, agrarian outlook suggests land stays with citizens, inferred.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Anachronistic; the movement defined liberty as protection from government action and would see discrimination as a matter of laws, not outcomes.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Republican theory held that luxury and love of wealth corrupt civic virtue; the movement stressed virtue and the plain middling sort, inferred.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: They feared standing armies and a strong national executive and favoured a defensive posture; inferred opposition to covert foreign wars.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Anachronistic; their dread of standing armies and consolidated power makes forcible intervention against an ally inferred as strongly rejected.

corporate-influence.rationale: The ratification debate did not address corporate lobbying; inferred as neutral.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Foreign funding of NGOs was not a ratification-era issue; inferred as neutral.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Population incentives were not discussed; inferred as neutral.

residents-only-property.rationale: Local self-government was favoured but land purchase limits were not addressed; inferred as neutral.

job-guarantee.rationale: Economic guarantees were not addressed in the ratification debate; inferred as neutral.

democratic-peace.rationale: The debate did not address democratic peace; inferred as neutral.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Inferred from the consent-based republicanism of Brutus and the Federal Farmer, under which laws bind through representation.

non-intervention.rationale: Foreign affairs were debated mainly through fear of standing armies; the question is inferred as neutral.

industrial-unions.rationale: Unions were not addressed in 1787-88; inferred as neutral.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Inferred from the demand for explicit rights protections for all citizens against rulers.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Marriage law was not part of the ratification debate; inferred as neutral.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Anti-Federalists objected to secrecy in the new government and wanted rulers visibly accountable to the people, as the Federal Farmer essays argue.

local-production.rationale: Local production was not addressed; inferred as neutral.

informal-organisation.rationale: Inferred from reliance on formal institutions such as state governments, numerous representatives and bills of rights.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Inferred from the insistence on local and state self-rule free of distant authority.

religious-nation.rationale: Several Anti-Federalists wanted religious tests but views varied; inferred as split.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Anti-Federalists wanted small republics of equal citizens and feared distant power; inferred from that, they would not favour ritual submission.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: They favoured local control of taxes and spending and feared consolidation, so regions keeping revenue fits their view, though this is inferred.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: They defended property rights as part of the liberty a bill of rights should protect, but did not address common ownership of production; inferred from that.

defeat-communism.rationale: Communism did not exist in 1787-88, and their concerns were domestic consolidation, so this is not addressed.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Their small-republic view favoured local and direct provision over remote administration, but the question was not addressed; a mild inference.

religion-illusion.rationale: Anti-Federalist writers assumed a religious people and valued virtue and religion in republics; inferred from that.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: They did not judge capitalism's historical role and many held agrarian suspicion of commerce, so adherents are split.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: The debate did not address women's status, and the Anti-Federalists sought change through law and representation; inferred from that.

socialized-care.rationale: Public domestic services were not discussed and would mean central or local power over families; inferred from their distrust of power.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Language policy was not debated, and their concern for liberty and local self-government counsels against state purging; inferred from that.

treaties-binding.rationale: They insisted on explicit limits that rulers cannot rewrite at will, so binding agreements fit their view, though treaties with internal nations were not discussed.

cooperative-communities.rationale: They favoured small self-governing republics but not common property, so the statement is only partly their view.

majority-settlement.rationale: Steering settlement into regions by state policy would extend consolidated power they feared; inferred from that.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: The question did not arise, and their preferred small agrarian republic with private property is not a third way; inferred from that.

missingStatements.text: A free republic can survive only over a small territory.
missingStatements.rationale: Brutus, following Montesquieu, argues a free republic cannot span a vast country, and this is the movement's defining argument.

missingStatements.text: A written bill of rights should limit what government may do.
missingStatements.rationale: Federal Farmer and the broader movement demanded explicit guarantees such as jury trial and a free press, leading to the Bill of Rights.

missingStatements.text: Officials should be required to rotate out of office after a limited time.
missingStatements.rationale: Federal Farmer No. 11 argues for rotation of legislators and a right of recall.

notes: Adherents differed on slavery, religion and commerce; the profile reflects the shared structural positions. Authorship of Brutus and Federal Farmer is uncertain.
